paragraphs.text: Windmills were constructed over 2,000 years ago in ancient Persia (Iran), where they were used to grind grain into flour. The first windmills could only face the direction of the prevailing wind. Centuries later in the Netherlands, modifications were made to the structure of windmills to permit their rotation, allowing them to face winds coming from variable directions. In Europe at this time the purpose of the windmill was still limited to grinding grain and raising water from wells, but these simple tasks were critical to the economy of the region. Subsequently, single windmills were used to drive generators, providing electricity for lighting and for storage batteries in buildings located in remote areas. But now, windmills are being utilized in whole new ways to help keep the planet safe. Today, wind farms, also called wind turbine farms, are seen as a viable way to produce energy and reduce carbon emissions at the same time. Wind energy is a pollution-free, infinitely sustainable form of energy. It doesn't use fuel, it doesn't produce greenhouse gases, and it doesn't produce toxins. Countries all over the world are utilizing modern windmills as a technology whose time has come.

Obviously, wind power must compete with conventional energy generation sources on a cost basis. In terms of power and energy, with any wind turbine, output increases dramatically as the wind speed increases. Therefore, the most cost-effective wind turbines are located in the windiest areas. Wind speed increases with height, so wind turbines are usually mounted on tall towers. Today, the lessons learned from more than a decade of operating wind power plants, along with continuing research and new developments, have made wind-generated electricity more economically feasible.

Modern wind turbine generators cost about $1500 per kilowatt for wind farms that operate several units of large machinery. Smaller individual units cost about $3000 per kilowatt. In good wind areas, the costs of generating electricity range between five and ten cents per kilowatt hour. That cost is somewhat higher than the costs associated with other sources, but wind energy costs are decreasing every year, whereas most conventional generation costs continue to increase because they depend on fossil fuels which are becoming more and more difficult and costly to extract from the earth. Wind power is also expected to grow worldwide because of favorable government policies.

The major challenge to using wind as a source of power is that the wind comes and goes and it does not always blow when electricity is needed. Wind energy cannot be stored (unless batteries are used) and not all winds can be harnessed to meet the timing of electricity demands. Denmark, which has the highest percentage of wind energy use of any nation (nearly 20%), has worked with this problem by connecting the Danish electrical grid to the grids of Germany, Sweden, and Norway. These interconnections allow Denmark to export electricity when wind power generation exceeds demand and import electricity when there is not enough wind.

Other challenges exist as well. Good wind sites are often located in remote locations, far from cities where the electricity is needed. Wind resource development may compete with other uses for the land. Although wind power plants have relatively little impact on the environment, there is some concern over the noise produced by the rotor blades. But the turbines are spread far apart and today they are quieter than a vacuum cleaner sound from the next room. Birds have also been killed by flying into the rotors. However, most of these problems have been resolved or greatly reduced through technological development or by properly siting wind plants.

Worldwide wind power generation has recently exceeded 200 billion kilowatt hours, which is equivalent to the annual electricity consumption of over 18 million average households in the United States. Overall, it has more than tripled in the last decade. This growth is mostly due to capacity increases in the United States, China, India, and Western Europe. But despite this growth, the world is still generating very little of the total electricity output from wind.

Over the past five years, the United States has led all other countries in wind power generation. The remaining top-ten wind power generators, listed in descending order, were China, Germany, Spain, India, Canada, the United Kingdom, France, Italy, and Denmark. Although about 60 countries have reported significant wind power generation, these top-ten countries have accounted for more than 85% of all wind generation worldwide. The growth in wind power generation has been particularly dramatic in China, where it has grown an average of 70% annually in the last decade, although this is still a relatively small proportion of the energy required there. For anyone who has seen majestic rows of tall turbines in the distance, it is clear that the story of wind power is only just beginning.

questions.prompt: Producing electricity from wind energy costs less than producing electricity through traditional methods.
Supply and demand problems are an obstacle for wind power producers.
Denmark exports more electricity than any other nation.
One problem with electricity distribution is the isolation of wind turbine sites.
More birds have been killed by flying into wind turbines than by other environmental hazards.
Most of the electricity being produced today worldwide comes from wind turbines.
European countries are leading the race in generating wind power.
